questions.question: What does it mean for $f\colon X\to Y$ to be surjective?
options: For every $y\in Y$, there exists $x\in X$ such that $f(x) = y$.
For every $x\in X$, there exists $y\in Y$ such that $f(x) = y$.
Different inputs must always give different outputs.
The domain and codomain must be the same set.
questions.explanation: f: X->Y is surjective when every y in Y has some x in X with f(x) = y (every codomain element is attained).
questions.source_support: Definition of surjective function.
option_explanations: That describes a function (every input has an output), not surjectivity.
Different inputs giving different outputs is injectivity, not surjectivity.
The domain and codomain need not be the same set.

questions.question: Which equivalent description of surjectivity is correct?
options: The codomain is exactly the range.
The domain is exactly the range.
The function has no repeated values.
questions.explanation: Surjectivity means the codomain is exactly the range (every element of Y is hit).
questions.source_support: Definition: onto means codomain equals range.

questions.question: Why does surjectivity depend on the codomain?
options: Because the codomain always equals the domain.
Because changing the codomain changes the formula of the function.
Because every element of the chosen codomain must be attained.
Because the range is ignored in surjectivity.
questions.explanation: Surjectivity depends on the codomain because every element of the chosen codomain must be attained (changing the codomain changes which elements need to be hit).
questions.source_support: Relevant result: changing the codomain may change surjectivity.

questions.question: What does surjectivity of $f\colon X\to Y$ require about $Y$?
options: No element of $X$ is allowed to map to the same value as another element.
Some elements of $Y$ must be outside the range.
No element of $Y$ is left unused by $f$.
The range must be smaller than the codomain.
questions.explanation: Surjectivity requires that no element of Y is left unused by f (every y in Y is f(x) for some x).
questions.skill_detail: surjection leaves no element of Y unused
questions.source_support: A surjection covers all of its codomain.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: That describes injectivity, not surjectivity.
Some elements outside the range means NOT surjective.
If the range is smaller than the codomain, the function is NOT surjective.

questions.question: Graphically, $f\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is surjective when every horizontal line $y=c$:
options: meets the graph at least once
meets the graph at most once
questions.explanation: Graphically, f: R->R is surjective when every horizontal line y=c meets the graph at least once.
questions.source_support: A surjection attains every element of its codomain.

Never meeting means the value c is not attained (not surjective).

questions.question: Let $f\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be $f(x)=x+1$. Is $f$ surjective?

questions.question: If $f$ and $g$ are surjective and $g\circ f$ is defined, is $g\circ f$ surjective?
questions.explanation: Yes, the composition of surjective functions is surjective (g being surjective ensures every element of the final codomain is attained).
questions.source_support: Surjectivity is preserved under composition.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: The composition of surjective functions IS surjective.

Surjectivity of $g\circ f$ follows from surjectivity of $f$ and $g$ alone, with no requirement that $f=g$; e.g. $f(x)=x^2\colon\mathbb{R}\to[0,\infty)$ and $g(y)=y\colon[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ give a surjective composition with $f\ne g$.
Injectivity is not required for the composition to be surjective.
